meta.ogDescription: Thucydides never wrote it. Cdr. W. B. Hayler invented the line at the Naval War College in 1960 and admitted the hoax in 1971.

answer.label: Not Thucydides — actually Cdr. W. B. ‘Bill’ Hayler, USN
answer.authorDates: U.S. Navy officer · coined the line in 1960 · confessed the prank in 1971
answer.sourceLine: Thucydides never wrote this. A U.S. Navy officer, then a student at the Naval War College, composed the line in 1960 and told everyone it came from “Volume IX of the Peloponnesian War” — a work that runs to only eight books. He posted it in the wardroom of his destroyer, it reached print in U.S. Naval Institute Proceedings in March 1962 still credited to Thucydides, and he owned up in a San Francisco newspaper column in February 1971.

source.excerpt: “A collision at Sea can ruin your entire day.” Thucydides 471-400 B.C. (Sign posted in wardroom of USS Buck DD-761) Submitted by Commander W.B. Hayler, U.S. Navy
trail: 1957 — the airborne ancestor. Speaking on air safety at a National Guard Association conference, Maj. Gen. Roger J. Browne, Jr. relayed a line from one of his jet-training headquarters: “A mid-air collision will ruin your entire day.” Quote Investigator calls this the earliest example of the class it has located ↗, and the phrase recurs in the Navy safety review Approach in 1958 and on the safety posters a 1960 novel describes.

March 1962 — the sea version reaches print. U.S. Naval Institute Proceedings runs the line as a page-foot filler, credited to Thucydides and sourced to a sign in the wardroom of USS Buck (DD-761) — submitted by Commander W. B. Hayler himself ↗. A Chicago newspaper boating column repeated it that September, and by 1966 it had been canonised in a naval quotation dictionary and quoted in Ebony in a profile of Commander Samuel L. Gravely.

14 February 1971 — the author confesses. Herb Caen’s San Francisco Chronicle column reports that Navy Capt. W. B. ‘Bill’ Hayler made it up at the Naval War College in 1960 because a professor “quoted him all day long”, and attributed it to a ninth volume of a work with eight. Fred R. Shapiro reproduced the column in full in 2010 ↗.
The negative check. The sentence is in no book of the History of the Peloponnesian War, which was subdivided into eight books ↗ and can be read end to end in English at Project Gutenberg ↗.
source.excerptNote: The filler item as transcribed by Quote Investigator from U.S. Naval Institute Proceedings, March 1962 — the earliest sea-collision version its researchers located, and submitted by the man who later admitted inventing it.

source.rightsHolder: W. B. Hayler or his estate; the March 1962 printing appeared in U.S. Naval Institute Proceedings (U.S. Naval Institute)
source.rightsNote: Because the line is not ancient text, no public-domain status can ride on Thucydides. Its author is identifiable — Hayler composed it in 1960 — and the earliest printing located is U.S. Naval Institute Proceedings of March 1962, comfortably after the 1931 U.S. public-domain cutoff, so it should be treated as in copyright to Hayler or his estate. A single-sentence maxim is thin material for any actual claim, but that is a judgement about enforceability, not about its date.

author.name: W. B. ‘Bill’ Hayler
author.kicker: The man who actually wrote it
author.heading: The prankster who out-quoted Thucydides
author.metaLine: U.S. Navy officer · Naval War College student, 1960 · commanding officer, USS Buck (DD-761)
author.bio: W. B. ‘Bill’ Hayler was a United States Navy officer who, by his own account, invented the most-quoted sentence in the maritime world while sitting through lectures at the Naval War College in 1960. His history professor, he said, was “absolutely hooked on Thucydides” and quoted him constantly — so Hayler wrote a line of deadpan understatement, credited it to a ninth volume of the Peloponnesian War that does not exist, and waited. He posted it on the bridge when he took command of the destroyer USS Buck, submitted it to U.S. Naval Institute Proceedings, and watched it escape: Reader’s Digest reprinted it and paid him five dollars, and Navy advertising put it in print as genuine. By 1971 he was a captain at the California Maritime Academy in Vallejo, and told columnist Herb Caen the whole thing was his.

misattribution.heading: Who gets the credit, and why they shouldn’t
misattribution.intro: This is a rare case where the hoaxer confessed in print, so the misattribution can be traced from invention to admission. It nonetheless still appears on wardroom plaques, in bridge notices and in quotation collections under the wrong name.

items.why: The line appears nowhere in the History of the Peloponnesian War. Wikiquote lists it in its Misattributed section ↗, recording that it was invented by a student at the US Naval War College in 1960 and then quoted as genuine Thucydides in Reader’s Digest in 1962.

Hayler built the tell into the joke: he told people it came from a ninth volume, and the History was subdivided into eight books ↗. Anyone who checked the reference would have caught it; for years nobody did.
New York magazine printed the maxim under that name in 1978. Quote Investigator says plainly that it does not know how or why Horowitz was linked to the saying ↗ — and neither do we.

Both forms circulate. The 1962 Proceedings filler and the Chicago newspaper reprint read “entire day”; the airborne ancestors of 1958 and 1960 read “whole day”, and Wikiquote lists the ‘whole day’ form ↗. No version is the ancient one, because there is no ancient one.

misattribution.truthLine: The idea is not Thucydidean and the words are not his: the sentence was written in 1960 by a U.S. Navy officer who said so himself in 1971 ↗, and it descends from mid-century American flight-safety posters rather than from fifth-century Athens.

context.heading: Why a fake ancient quote outran the real ones
lead: The joke works because the sentence sounds exactly like what a modern reader expects an ancient Greek to sound like: flat, unhurried, faintly grim. That is also what made it unfalsifiable in practice. Nobody carrying a card in a wardroom was going to open eight books of Athenian naval history to check, and the false citation — a ninth volume — was designed to send anyone who did to a shelf that ends one book earlier.

Its real family tree is American and airborne. Quote Investigator traces the pattern to 1957, when a general quoted the line “A mid-air collision will ruin your entire day” from one of his own jet-training commands; the Navy’s aviation safety review printed a version in 1958, and a 1960 novel about commercial aviation refers to it as an old safety poster. Hayler’s contribution was to move it from the air to the sea and give it a 2,400-year-old author.
context.detailsSummary: How far it got before anyone checked
detailsBody: Hayler’s own tally of the spread, given to Herb Caen in 1971: he posted it on the bridge when he took command of USS Buck in 1960; Reader’s Digest picked it up in 1962 and paid him five dollars; and Navy advertising for a rules-of-the-road publication ran the quotation as genuine.

Independently of Hayler’s account, the attribution kept propagating through respectable channels: a boating column in the Chicago Daily Tribune in September 1962 relayed it from Proceedings as a comment “originated by Thucydides”; a 1966 Dictionary of Military and Naval Quotations filed it under “Collision” as “Attributed to Thucydides”; and a 1966 Ebony profile described Commander Samuel L. Gravely keeping a card with the line on it.

The maxim also mutated back toward the air. During Apollo 10 in 1969, commander Thomas P. Stafford, discussing the discarded lunar module stage below the spacecraft, remarked that a collision was highly improbable but “would sure ruin your whole day if it happened.”
context.pull: “Of course, Thucydides only wrote eight volumes.” — Capt. W. B. Hayler, 1971

sourcesVerified.claim: Quote Investigator concludes the maxim was created and disseminated as a prank by Commander W. B. ‘Bill’ Hayler, who confessed he initiated it while a student at the Naval War College in 1960; the earliest sea-collision citation QI located is U.S. Naval Institute Proceedings, March 1962, submitted by Hayler and sourced to a sign in the wardroom of USS Buck DD-761 credited to “Thucydides 471-400 B.C.”; the earliest example of the class located is a 1957 mid-air version from Maj. Gen. Roger J. Browne, Jr.; later spread includes the Chicago Daily Tribune (Sept 1962), the Dictionary of Military and Naval Quotations (1966), Ebony (1966, Cdr. Samuel L. Gravely), Apollo 10 (1969) and “Horowitz’s First Law of the Admiralty” in New York magazine (1978), about which QI says it does not know how or why Horowitz was linked.

Wikiquote lists “A collision at sea can ruin your whole day” under its Misattributed section for Thucydides, noting it was ascribed to Book IX — a clue that it is a joke, as Thucydides wrote only eight books — that it was invented by a student at the US Naval War College in 1960, and that it was quoted as genuine in Reader’s Digest in 1962.

Fred R. Shapiro’s “Quotes Uncovered: When Ships Collide” (8 July 2010) reproduces Herb Caen’s San Francisco Chronicle column of 14 February 1971, in which Navy Capt. W. B. ‘Bill’ Hayler of the California Maritime Academy in Vallejo confesses he made the saying up at the Naval War College in 1960, told everybody it was from Volume IX of the Peloponnesian War although Thucydides wrote only eight volumes, posted it on the bridge of USS Buck, and that Reader’s Digest picked it up in 1962 and paid him five dollars.
Project Gutenberg hosts the complete English text of Thucydides’ History of the Peloponnesian War in Richard Crawley’s translation.
Thucydides (c. 460 – c. 400 BC) was an Athenian historian and general, and after his death his History was subdivided into eight books.
The Perseus Digital Library hosts the full text of Thucydides’ Peloponnesian War, navigable as eight books.
Proceedings is a magazine published by the U.S. Naval Institute, launched in 1874.
